title: The vendor integration request — question explanation
learningObjective: Assess supplier access, assurance evidence and data-handling obligations
format: 16:9 educational motion-graphics video; narration; separate captions; no autoplay with sound
visualStyle: Deep navy and charcoal; restrained cyan/electric-blue highlights; limited purple accents; clean typography; purposeful, low-motion transitions; accessible contrast.

scenes.name: Scenario setup
scenes.visual: A supplier asks for broad administrator access to your cloud tenant to troubleshoot an integration. The contract does not clearly describe data processing, logging or access termination.
scenes.direction: Show a fictional simulated setting. Use generic UI and no actual organization, brand, user identity, credential, real URL or live account.

scenes.name: Learning objective and risk cue
scenes.visual: Assess supplier access, assurance evidence and data-handling obligations
scenes.direction: Highlight only observable cues and explain the decision context without implying certainty beyond the scenario.

scenes.name: Recommended response
scenes.visual: Option A: Complete supplier/security review, define data and access scope, use named time-bound least-privilege accounts, log activity and document offboarding. Supplier access should be constrained, attributable, monitored and governed by explicit contractual and technical controls.
scenes.direction: Animate the recommended defensive choice as a clear decision path. Display the action verb and trusted channel/control.

scenes.name: Why the other options fail
scenes.visual: Option B: Broad access before due diligence expands exposure and can be difficult to unwind. Option C: Shared credentials reduce accountability and create an insecure secret-distribution path. Option D: A verbal promise without enforceable scope and technical controls is insufficient.
scenes.direction: Show each unsafe alternative separately with a complete, concise reason. Do not depict operational exploitation, malicious code or credential capture.

scenes.name: Defensive takeaway
scenes.visual: Delay access until procurement, security, privacy and system owners document the supplier’s need, safeguards, data terms, account scope and revocation plan. Third-party trust must be supported by evidence, scoped access, monitoring and lifecycle controls.
scenes.direction: Close with one readable takeaway and the next safe action. Keep the final frame long enough for comprehension.
scenes.onScreenText: Third-party trust must be supported by evidence, scoped access, monitoring and lifecycle controls.

narration: Scenario: A supplier asks for broad administrator access to your cloud tenant to troubleshoot an integration. The contract does not clearly describe data processing, logging or access termination. Safest response: Option A: Complete supplier/security review, define data and access scope, use named time-bound least-privilege accounts, log activity and document offboarding. Supplier access should be constrained, attributable, monitored and governed by explicit contractual and technical controls. Option B is unsafe because Broad access before due diligence expands exposure and can be difficult to unwind. Option C is unsafe because Shared credentials reduce accountability and create an insecure secret-distribution path. Option D is unsafe because A verbal promise without enforceable scope and technical controls is insufficient. In practice: Delay access until procurement, security, privacy and system owners document the supplier’s need, safeguards, data terms, account scope and revocation plan. Key takeaway: Third-party trust must be supported by evidence, scoped access, monitoring and lifecycle controls.

generationInstructions: Use the narration as the voiceover source; preserve its meaning and do not add unsupported technical claims.
Render a 16:9 MP4 at 1080p or equivalent; keep text inside safe margins.
Use only fictional names, domains, screens and values. Never render real secrets, OTPs, account data or real target systems.
Provide a separate WebVTT caption file and transcript; do not rely on burned-in text alone.
Use no flashing effects, rapid strobing, unnecessary parallax or autoplay audio.
Human-review the rendered video for factual accuracy, spelling, pronunciation, captions and timing before marking it validated.
accessibility: Separate synchronized captions and transcript required. Written explanation is the fallback. Avoid flashing and color-only information. Provide a static equivalent of all essential 3D visuals.
